title: Variables
description: Creating variables, types (string, number, boolean), and printing

exercises.title: What is a Variable?
exercises.content: A variable is a named container that stores a value. In Python, you create one by writing a name, then =, then the value. No special keyword needed — just pick a name and assign!

highlights.note: Creates a variable called 'name' and stores the text "Morey" in it.
Creates a variable called 'age' and stores the number 10 in it. Numbers don't need quotes.
print() shows what's stored inside a variable.

exercises.title: Types of Values
exercises.content: Variables can store different types of values. The three main types are: strings (text in quotes), integers (whole numbers), and floats (decimal numbers). Python figures out the type automatically based on what you assign.
exercises.code:
name = "Alice"
age = 12
height = 4.5
print(name)
print(age)
print(height)

highlights.note: Strings are text — always surrounded by quotes (single or double).
Integers are whole numbers — no quotes, no decimal point.
Floats are decimal numbers — they have a dot in them.

exercises.title: Changing Variables
exercises.content: You can change what's stored in a variable by assigning it a new value. The old value is gone — replaced by the new one. The variable always holds whatever was assigned to it most recently.
exercises.code:
score = 0
print(score)
score = 10
print(score)
score = 25
print(score)

highlights.note: Now score is 10 — the 0 is gone forever.
Now score is 25. A variable always holds its most recent value.

exercises.title: Using Variables Together
exercises.content: Variables can be used in calculations with other variables. Python reads the current value of each variable and does the math. You can also combine strings together using + (this is called concatenation).
exercises.code:
width = 4
height = 3
area = width * height
print(area)

first = "Hello "
last = "world"
message = first + last
print(message)

highlights.note: Python reads width (4) and height (3), multiplies them, and stores 12 in 'area'.
The + operator joins strings together. "Hello " + "world" becomes "Hello world".
